body.text: Japan’s robotics sector finds itself at a critical juncture. After losing market share to Chinese firms in recent years, Japan now faces an additional threat: possible trade restrictions from the United States. The Trump administration recently announced that advanced robotics and industrial machinery imports threaten U.S. national security. Although no tariffs have been announced yet, the administration ordered the U.S. Trade Representative to negotiate acceptable trade agreements within 180 days.

The news is not all bad. The launch of negotiations presents an opportunity to deepen cooperation, not restrict it. Japan and the U.S. have strong economic and strategic incentives to build an allied market for advanced robotics and industrial automation. Making that market a reality will require new rules — and a new way of thinking about technology competition.

The economic logic for cooperation is straightforward. The U.S. is a global leader in artificial intelligence and advanced computing. Meanwhile, Japan has cutting-edge expertise in physical hardware. Together, the two nations can create a complete industrial ecosystem that spans all the way from design to development to deployment.

The strategic reasons for cooperation are also clear. China is winning the global deployment race, combining unmatched manufacturing scale and state-directed investment to expand its market share. In 2025, China installed five times as many industrial robots as Japan and the U.S. combined. And this is not just in lower-end products. China’s state-subsidized firms are rapidly moving up the value chain to compete in high-end automation.

In response, Japan has already made physical AI a policy priority at home. Abroad, the groundwork for bilateral cooperation has been laid through the U.S.-Japan Technology Prosperity Deal. The next step is establishing Japan as a trusted U.S. partner.

Building that trust means overcoming two regulatory barriers. The first is U.S. domestic content rules. In July, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) added advanced robotic devices to its Covered List and required that more than 65 percent domestic content to escape restrictions – a threshold set to rise to 75 percent by 2029.

Under current rules, a robot built with Japanese components could fail this test even though they pose no significant security risk. A collaborative robot that relies on Japanese-made servomotors could be penalized simply because it contains foreign parts. As a result, Tokyo should press Washington to recognize a “trusted allied-content credit,” allowing Japanese-made components to count toward domestic content thresholds. This would preserve safeguards against Chinese penetration of the market while also securing Japan’s access to U.S. buyers.

The second regulatory barrier is fragmentated product certification standards. Japan and the United States utilize different security standards and verification processes. The two countries do not need to use precisely the same standards to facilitate trade, but instead, Japan should advocate for the mutual recognition of security testing. For example, a robot certified as secure in Nagoya should not face a redundant, costly certification process in the U.S. Co-developing security testing protocols and shared certification schemes can lower compliance costs for its exporters.

These barriers are high, but Japan enters negotiations with considerable leverage. American manufacturers depend heavily on Japanese industrial components to automate domestic production. Restricting Japanese access would raise costs for U.S. factories and undermine competitiveness on both sides of the Pacific. For example, Japan’s AI-enabled precision robots – such as Kawasaki Heavy Industries’ automated welding systems or Nabtesco’s precision reduction gears – offer potential to enhance efficiency of critical industries like naval shipbuilding and semiconductor fabrication.
Therefore, Tokyo has a strong case that integrating Japanese products strengthens, rather than weakens, the U.S. industrial base.

The benefits of Japan-U.S. cooperation extend beyond the bilateral partnership. A Japan-U.S. robotics agreement can have knock-on benefits for broader cooperation in the region. Outside of just Japan and the United States, South Korean semiconductors and Taiwanese chips could also help expand a trusted network of technology builders and buyers.

Achieving that level of cooperation will not be easy, especially given the political landscape within the U.S. Even the Democratic Party’s midterm victory is unlikely to suddenly reverse the United States’ protectionist attitudes. U.S. trade policy is still gripped by manufacturing lobbies focused on reshoring critical, strategically sensitive production.
But the strategic risks of failing to cooperate should outweigh other concerns. Only integration can ensure a safe, secure technology stack from top to bottom – and from east to west.
